title: Fathers with Pouches
subject: seahorses: slow swimming, gripping, feeding, and male pregnancy
passage:
With its horse-shaped head and curled tail, a seahorse looks more like a small carving than a fish. But it is a fish, and one of the strangest in the sea.

Seahorses are poor swimmers. A small fin on the back flutters very fast to push them along, and two tiny fins near the head help them steer. Because they move so slowly, they spend much of their time holding still. A seahorse wraps its tail around a stalk of seagrass or a branch of coral and stays put, sometimes for hours.

Holding still has its uses. A seahorse eats tiny shrimp and other small animals that drift past. It waits until one comes close, then sucks it up through its long snout, like a drink through a straw. Many seahorses can also change color to match their surroundings, which helps them stay hidden.

The most surprising thing about seahorses is which parent carries the babies. The female places her eggs in a pouch on the male's belly. The male carries the eggs for several weeks while they develop. Then he gives birth, pushing out dozens or even hundreds of tiny seahorses, each small enough to sit on a fingernail.

From the moment they are born, the young are on their own. They drift away to find a grip of their own in the seagrass.

title: Inside a Zipper
subject: how a zipper's teeth and slider lock and unlock
exclusion_greps: zipper: mentions only (repair cafe, airport), no zipper explainer
passage:
You probably zip a jacket or a backpack every day without thinking about it. Inside that quick motion is a small, clever machine.

A zipper has two rows of teeth, one on each side of the opening. Each tooth has a tiny bump on top and a matching hollow underneath. The teeth on one side sit halfway between the teeth on the other side, like the fingers of two hands ready to fold together.

The part you pull is called the slider. Inside it are two channels at the top that join into one channel at the bottom, in the shape of the letter Y. When you pull the slider up, the two rows of teeth are squeezed together as they pass through the Y. Each bump presses into the hollow of a tooth from the other row, and the teeth lock into a tight chain.

When you pull the slider down, a small wedge inside it pushes the teeth apart again, one by one, and the zipper opens.

The zipper took a long time to get right. An early version was patented in the 1890s, but it often came apart. Around 1913, an engineer named Gideon Sundback designed a version with neat rows of interlocking teeth, much like the zipper used today. The name "zipper" came along in the 1920s and is said to imitate the sound it makes.

title: How a Dandelion Seed Flies
subject: the swirling ring of air that keeps a dandelion seed aloft (2018 Edinburgh study)

passage:
When you blow on a dandelion gone to seed, dozens of tiny parachutes lift into the air. Each one carries a single seed, and some of them travel remarkably far.

A dandelion seed hangs beneath a puff of about one hundred thin bristles, which scientists call a pappus. For a long time, people assumed the puff worked like a small umbrella, catching the air beneath it. Then, in 2018, researchers at the University of Edinburgh looked more closely, using a wind tunnel and high-speed cameras.

What they found surprised them. Air flowing up through the gaps between the bristles forms a ring of swirling air that floats just above the puff, without touching it. This ring increases the drag on the seed and slows its fall. The bristles are spaced so that the ring stays steady instead of breaking apart.

The design is remarkably efficient. Because the puff is mostly empty space, it is very light, yet the researchers reported that it slows the seed far more efficiently, for its weight, than a solid parachute would. Most seeds still land within a few meters of the plant. On a breezy day, though, a few can be carried for long distances.

The researchers reported that this kind of flight had not been described in nature before. Some engineers now wonder whether tiny flying devices, such as small sensors, could one day be built the same way.

title: Beads That Count
subject: counting boards, the suanpan and the soroban
passage:
Long before calculators, people found ways to make arithmetic easier with their hands.

Some of the earliest tools were counting boards. In parts of the ancient world, including Greece and Rome, people drew lines on a flat surface and moved small stones or tokens between them. Each line stood for a place value, such as ones, tens, or hundreds. The Latin word for a small stone, calculus, is where we get the word "calculate."

Over time, many cultures turned the counting board into a frame of beads that slide along rods. In China, a version called the suanpan was in wide use several hundred years ago. It usually has two beads above a crossbar and five below on each rod. Later, the Japanese soroban simplified the design to one bead above and four below, which is enough to show any digit from zero to nine.

The idea behind every abacus is the same. Each rod stands for a place value, and the position of the beads shows the digit in that place. To add, a user pushes beads toward the crossbar; to carry a ten, the user clears a rod and moves one bead on the next rod to the left.

Skilled users can work astonishingly fast. Some students who train for years learn to picture an abacus in their minds and move imaginary beads to solve problems, with no frame in front of them at all.

title: Wangari Maathai and the Green Belt
subject: Wangari Maathai and the Green Belt Movement
passage:
When Wangari Maathai was a child in the highlands of Kenya, she was told never to cut down a certain fig tree near her home. Its roots, the adults said, held the soil together and helped the nearby stream run clear.

She grew up to become a scientist. In 1971 she earned a doctorate from the University of Nairobi, becoming the first woman in East and Central Africa to earn that degree. But as she traveled through the countryside, she saw trouble. Forests had been cut down for farms and firewood. Streams were drying up, and women had to walk farther each day to find wood for cooking.

Maathai believed part of the answer could be as simple as planting trees. In 1977 she began what became the Green Belt Movement. The group paid women a small amount for each seedling they raised that survived. The trees would give families firewood and fruit, hold the soil in place, and shade the streams.

The work was hard, and at times it was dangerous. Maathai spoke out when powerful people tried to take public land for themselves, and she was arrested more than once for her protests. She kept going.

Over the following decades, the women of the Green Belt Movement planted tens of millions of trees. In 2004, Maathai was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize, the first African woman to receive it. She argued that caring for the land and keeping the peace were connected, because people fight over resources when those resources grow scarce.

title: Armor That Is Not Enough
subject: pangolins: scales, defense, diet, and trafficking
passage:
A pangolin looks like a walking pinecone. From its nose to the tip of its tail, its body is covered in overlapping scales, and it is the only mammal with a coat like that.

The scales are made of keratin, the same material as human fingernails. They are hard and sharp-edged, and they make an excellent defense. When a pangolin is threatened, it curls into a tight ball, tucking its soft belly and face inside. A lion or a leopard that finds a curled pangolin may bat it around for a while, but it usually cannot break through.

Pangolins need that armor, because they lead slow, solitary lives. The eight species live in parts of Africa and Asia, and most come out at night. They feed almost entirely on ants and termites. A pangolin rips open a nest with its strong front claws and then catches the insects with an extremely long, sticky tongue. Pangolins have no teeth. Instead, they swallow small stones and grit, which help grind up food inside their stomachs.

The same armor that protects pangolins from lions has made them a target for people. Their scales are used in some traditional medicines, and their meat is sold in some places as a luxury. Because curling into a ball does nothing to stop a person who simply picks it up, pangolins are easy to catch. Conservation groups describe them as among the most trafficked mammals in the world.

Today, all eight species are protected by an international agreement that bans commercial trade in them. Groups in several countries rescue pangolins taken from smugglers, care for them, and return them to the wild. Whether those efforts will be enough is still uncertain.

title: The Stairs That Fold Away
subject: how an escalator's chains, tracks, comb plate and handrail work
passage:
An escalator seems to make stairs rise out of the floor, carry you up, and then swallow the stairs again at the top. In fact, the same steps go around and around in a giant loop.

The steps are attached to a pair of chains that run in a continuous loop, like a bicycle chain stretched out on a slant. A motor, usually hidden beneath the top landing, turns large gears that move the chains. As the chains move, the steps travel with them: up along the top of the loop, then back down underneath, upside down and out of sight.

The clever part is how the steps change shape. Each step has two pairs of small wheels, and each pair rides on its own track. Along the slanted middle section, the two tracks are far apart in height, so the back of each step sits higher than its front edge would, and the steps form a staircase. Near the top and bottom, the tracks come together at the same height, and the steps flatten into a smooth platform that is easy to step on and off.

At each end, a metal comb plate meets the steps. Its teeth fit into grooves on the surface of each step, guiding the steps under the floor and helping keep shoelaces and other objects from being pulled in.

The handrail is a loop of its own, driven by the same machinery so that it moves at nearly the same speed as the steps. If the handrail ran much slower or faster, riders would feel their hands pulled ahead of or behind their feet, which is why engineers check its speed carefully.

title: Records Made of Knots
subject: Inca khipus and how their knots record numbers
passage:
The Inca Empire stretched along the mountains of western South America in the 1400s and early 1500s, and it ran one of the largest states of its time. It collected taxes, counted its people, and stored food in thousands of warehouses. Yet as far as historians can tell, it had no system of writing like the ones used in Europe or China.

Instead, the Inca kept records on khipus (also spelled quipus), bundles of knotted cords. A khipu has one main cord with many thinner cords hanging from it, sometimes hundreds. Some of those cords have smaller cords tied to them in turn. The cords came in different colors, and the color may have shown what was being counted.

In the early 1900s, a researcher named Leland Locke showed that many khipus record numbers using place value, much like our own system. Knots near the bottom of a cord stand for ones, the next cluster up for tens, then hundreds, and so on. Different kinds of knots, including long knots with several turns, show the digits. An empty space on the cord stands for zero.

Reading and making khipus was a job for trained record keepers, called khipukamayuq. Spanish writers who arrived in the 1500s described these keepers reciting long accounts, and even histories, from their cords.

That detail is one reason some researchers suspect that khipus recorded more than numbers: perhaps names, places, or even stories. So far, nobody has been able to prove it. Several hundred khipus survive in museums today, and scholars are still working to read the ones whose knots seem to break the rules of the number system.

title: Quiet the Leaf Blowers
subject: phasing out gas-powered leaf blowers in a town, with a counterclaim about landscaping crews
exclusion_greps: light-pollution and four-day-week essays exist; different topics
passage:
Every Saturday morning on my street, the leaf blowers start before the birds are finished singing. One neighbor runs his for an hour to clear a driveway that a rake could finish in twenty minutes. I think it is time for our town to phase out gas-powered leaf blowers.

The first reason is noise. A gas blower is loud enough to bother people several houses away, and its low, droning sound travels through walls and windows. For workers who use them all day, the noise can damage their hearing, especially when they work without ear protection.

The second reason is pollution. Many gas leaf blowers use small engines that burn fuel far less cleanly than a modern car. By some estimates, running a commercial blower for an hour can release more of certain pollutants than driving a car for hundreds of miles. Blowers also kick dust, pollen, and dried animal waste into the air we breathe.

Some people argue that limits would hurt landscaping crews, who depend on fast equipment to finish many yards a day. That concern is fair. Electric blowers cost money, and their batteries have to be charged. A small crew cannot simply buy a whole new set of tools overnight.

But the answer is to help those crews, not to keep the problem. Several towns that have limited gas blowers have phased in their rules over a few years and offered discounts on electric equipment. Our town could do the same: set a date a few years away, help small businesses pay for new tools, and allow exceptions for heavy cleanups after storms.

Fall leaves are one of the best parts of the season. The roar that chases them should not be.

title: Garrett Morgan's Pause
subject: Garrett Morgan: safety hood, the Lake Erie tunnel rescue, and his traffic signal
passage:
Garrett Morgan had only an elementary school education, but he had a mind that kept asking how things could work better.

Morgan was born in Kentucky in 1877, the son of parents who had been enslaved. As a teenager he moved north to Ohio, eventually settling in Cleveland, where he found work repairing sewing machines. He was good at it, and he was curious. Within a few years he had opened his own repair shop and later a clothing business.

His most dramatic invention was a breathing device he called a safety hood. The wearer pulled a canvas hood over the head, and a long tube hanging down drew in air from near the ground, where smoke is usually thinner. Morgan patented the hood in 1914 and showed how it worked by walking into tents filled with thick smoke.

In 1916, an explosion trapped workers in a tunnel being dug under Lake Erie. Morgan and his brother put on safety hoods, went into the tunnel, and helped carry men out. Newspapers at first gave little credit to the two Black men who had led part of the rescue, an injustice that Morgan spoke about for years.

Morgan's best-known idea came from the street. In the early 1920s, Cleveland's roads were crowded with cars, horse-drawn wagons, bicycles, and people on foot, and many traffic signals of the day switched from stop to go with no warning in between. According to many accounts, Morgan designed a signal after seeing a bad collision at an intersection. His signal had an extra position that stopped traffic in every direction for a moment before the signal changed. He received a patent for it in 1923 and later sold the rights to General Electric.

That brief pause, a moment when everyone waits, serves the same purpose as the warning light in the signals we use today.
